title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
hook: the music stops, a flame is lit on a plate, and everyone reaches toward it with both hands

segments.voice: Yesterday's kirtan repertoire song: the Goddess in all beings, in peace and compassion, and in hunger, sleep and error too. Hunger, bow. Error, bow.

Late in the evening the drum goes quiet. Someone lights a small flame on a brass plate, a wick in ghee or a piece of camphor, and stands before the image at the front of the room. The plate moves in slow circles while a bell rings in the other hand. The room stands and starts a song some of them clearly know by heart. When the circling stops, the plate is carried through the room. People reach out with both hands, pass their palms over the flame, and draw the warmth back over their eyes and the top of the head.
screen: `THE DRUM GOES QUIET.` → `A FLAME ON A BRASS PLATE.` → `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, TO THE EYES.`

segments.voice: That's aarti: light waved before the deity, often as the closing act of a puja or a kirtan. The song sung with it is also called an aarti, and one of the aartis sung in Hindi is Om jai jagdish hare. Tradition credits the words to a Punjabi writer, Shardha Ram Phillauri. The opening, in paraphrase: Om, victory to you, Lord of the world, Hari, who removes in a moment the troubles of your devotees. Later comes a line that's easy to sing and hard to forget: you are my mother and my father; with whom else would I take shelter? Look where the evening has gone. It began with Ganesha, clearing the road. Then Shiva, a bow to everything. Then Rama's name, a lamp on the tongue. Then Krishna's names, sung as a call. Then the Goddess, found even in hunger and error. Now the light itself is carried round, and people take it into their hands. A kirtan repertoire isn't just a playlist. It has a shape: from beginning, through bowing and naming and calling, to receiving. One way to read the gesture at the end: the light offered up comes back to each person in the room. Families differ on the details, which aarti, which lamp, how many circles, and none of that needs settling here. The songs go out, the light comes back.
screen: `AARTI: LIGHT WAVED, A SONG SUNG.` · `YOU ARE MY MOTHER AND MY FATHER.` · `A REPERTOIRE HAS A SHAPE.` · `THE LIGHT COMES BACK TO EACH PERSON.` · then, large: `THE SONGS GO OUT. THE LIGHT COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: If there's a candle or a lamp nearby, you can light it, safely; if not, any light will do, a window or a screen dimmed low. Hold your palms toward it and feel whatever warmth or brightness reaches them, then slowly bring them back to rest over your closed eyes for a moment. If you pray, let this be your aarti; if not, let it be a moment of receiving something you didn't make.
Kirtan repertoire. The songs a group knows by heart, and the shape they make: from Ganesha at the start to the aarti, the light carried round at the end.
Your line: the light comes back. Tomorrow, a new road: jnana, the way of knowing. That's day nine hundred ninety-two.

chat.says: At the end of the kirtan, why does everyone touch the flame and then their eyes?
options: The aarti light is offered up, then carried round so it comes back to each person.
It's to check the flame is still lit before the plate goes back to the front.
It's a way to cool the hands after so much clapping during the songs.
chat.meaning: In aarti the lamp is waved before the deity, then carried round. One reading: the light offered up comes back to each person.
